So, one of our flips was one of our comps here. I put in a couple more in here for them, but it kind of triggered my memory that I never did this [music] video for you guys on the breakdown on this deal. So, here's the numbers. I want to go over the numbers with you guys. So, as I said, we locked it up for 175, commissions and referral fees. So, this is what I do when I buy a property that I'm I'm ready to flip. First of all, I want to make sure at least 30% or more [music] of the properties listed in this area are pending. This one in particular had like 70-80% of the properties pending, so I knew it was safe. I knew it was a good market and if we did a good job on the flip, we could sell this thing fast. So, it starts with a realtor because if you can find the best realtor that lists all the flips in this area, then they're going to have all the contacts for photos, for inspections, for contractors, subcontractors. Uh they know the market well. They know what finishes to do on this property. So, you're going to get the most money for it. So, always start with the best agent in the area. So, I called three of them. Uh two did not answer. One did. And I talked about the flips that she had listed. She actually was an investor herself. I said, "Hey, I'm under contract on this house. So, I borrowed the money against myself. My money makes about 10% in the market, and I borrowed against it at 5%, so I'm still making 5% net on my money as I was working with it on this flip. So, I borrowed 200 grand from myself. on this for 175. I already had an agent in place. I already had her contractors in place. I already had an estimate in place. So, we ended up getting going on the rehab the day I closed on it because all all my my ducks were in a row. So, close on it, do the rehab. It took about 30 days to do the rehab, and I'll show you guys photos of what this property looked like when we bought it, and I'll show you the photos on once it was cleaned up. So, these are the original photos that we took on this property when we first got it under contract here in the office. So, it's a nice house, two-car garage, siding was good. Everything looks good on it. So, one thing that we did have to do was kind of clean up all these posts from an old deck that was taken out. So, we [music] did that in the rehab. I'll show you guys. We had to take out whatever the hell this was like cabling uh that they had put in there. We had a pressure wash all the siding. These were were rotted out. So we ended [music] up having to replace those. That's something that came up later once we started the rehab. There's our seller right there and some double and you know it was pretty cosmetic. We didn't didn't do much to this. We had to we knew we had to redo the floors. We had to paint everything. That was a given. We had to replace a lot of plumbing and lighting fixtures but that to me is still just all a lipstick rehab. There was no major components that that we had to do. The roof was good. HVAC was good. It just needed a little bit of a face-lift. So this is everything. We had to you know get all the clutter out of there. Get rid of some of these cheap broken light fixtures. Obviously the carpet's bad. Doors needed to be painted and cleaned. Washer and dryer was left there. As you can see this door has seen better days. You guys kind of get the picture here. And then let's look at the Zillow listing. And then as you can tell we had you know you get a good agent that lists a lot of flips and and sells a lot of deals and up getting really cool photos for you. So this was the photos after we rehabbed it. All new posts and wood on the front there like I had said. They cleaned up the yard and then we did all LVP flooring throughout. When it came to the color the finish of the LVP I left that up to my realtor cuz I said hey you're going to know what's going to sell faster and she went with this light kind of vintage lighter color. Obviously we usually go with agreeable gray. We painted the door black. We kept some of the lighting fixtures replaced others. We replaced all the the outlets and and covers just to make it look nice. One thing we didn't do cuz it wasn't really needed is do anything with the kitchen. So, now when I do flips like on this one, I'm just looking at other properties that are selling for the price range I need and I'm not doing anything I don't need to do. Reason being is because during COVID and all that craze of the real estate market, when interest rates were like 2 or 3%, all these VA and FHA buyers were just getting beat by conventional buyers and cash buyers because there's way less contingencies in those types of offers. And those well-qualified buyers typically had a little bit more money, so they were offering over list price cuz they could put more money into the deal. So, for a long time when interest rates were low, these FHA and VA buyers were just getting outbid on properties. Found the agent, used all her contacts, got estimates, closed on it, did the rehab, listed it, and sold it within 90 days. Made about $32,000. You can do this a lot of different ways with the money. Um, you can borrow private money. You can take a line of credit out on on your mortgage. Um, you can borrow money from yourself if you have a brokerage account. You could use a hard money lender, which I use a lot of those as well. Um, but for this particular one, tried it out borrowing money from myself and it worked out beautifully. But always find the best agent, use them as your property or project manager, and make sure whatever kind of flip rehab you're doing, it matches what's selling out there in this area. Don't overdo it, don't underdo it. Like you want this to move fast and go super smooth, but don't cut any corners, either. Like when you're doing the rehab, if you know something's going to come up in an inspection, make sure you just fix it now, so there's not a huge negotiation while you're under contract with a buyer. Like just fix it, you're going to have to fix it anyway, and just get it done. One thing I did not do on this property, which I should have, and is the second time I forgot to do it, was get homeowner's insurance while I was under contract. So the whole time I owned this property for 3 months, I never had insurance on it. So if this thing burnt to the ground, I would've been out $200,000, cuz I didn't have insurance on it. So shame on me for not doing that, but I didn't do it on this one, and I forgot to do it on another one in North Carolina. I actually sent all the information to my insurance company, they sent me a quote, and I forgot to call them back and and tell them to to just charge the card. So that was my fault. Another thing, you got to switch all the utilities, and you got to make sure you you switch them when when you sell it as well. But always get homeowner's insurance, learn from me, cuz I could've lost big on this one. But again, you guys can do this. If you're wholesaling a lot of the deals, make sure you're stacking some of that cash, so you have some free capital to do this kind of stuff. When we originally sent this deal out, the highest offer we had made this deal a $15,000 deal, okay? For very little work and a little bit more time, I made 32, almost $32,000 on this, and it was very little effort. Making taking a couple phone calls here and there, but having a really good agent in the area really helps. So, as you guys continue this journey, make sure you're looking at your deals like this. Start flipping some no-brainer properties where you cannot lose. And as long as you can make 15-20% on any money you do have in the deal, it's a good deal. So, guys, if you like this video, you like my content, make sure you like and subscribe. Make sure you comment. Let me know what you think of this and what you want on future videos. And make sure you share this as well. I'll see you guys at the top.

videos.title: The Exact Daily Schedule That Scaled My Wholesaling Team (Focuses on the "blueprint" )
videos.transcript: Today, I want to talk about a training schedule for yourself or your team, whether you're a one-man band or you're currently scaling and hiring people. But, I want to give you guys a blueprint of what we do in my office every single day to train and get better on the phones, whether it's acquisitions or dispositions. I'll go over our training schedule here in our office, and I want to give you guys some KPIs that you can go by with you or your team. This is going to get you contracts and get you that consistency that you need in any business, okay? And this relates to any sales job. Before we get started, though, make sure you're subscribing and you're liking and you're commenting on everything so we can grow this channel and help more people. I really appreciate it. What's up, guys? Hopefully, you're enjoying this content. I do want to announce that we have the winners for the December giveaway. Sorry, it's a couple months late, but we do have the winners, first, second, and third place. So, please stay till the end of the video to see if you won. Remember, this is everybody that liked and commented and subscribed to every single post in December, so we finally have the winners. Stay till the end so you know if you won, and I will see you guys at the top. So, I'm going to give you at the end of this video a PDF of exactly what we train on every single day, and I want to go over that with you. So, in wholesaling and acquisitions, you're only as good as you can get by training every single day. Now, I look at a schedule, a routine as just doing everything every day. When I go to the gym, I just do it every day. If I'm working out, I do it every single day. The less we do it, the less we get out of our routine, we give ourselves excuses to not do it. I'll boil it down to the gym. If I said, "Hey, every week I'm going to work out three times a week." Well, if I said Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and my Wednesday was really busy, I would make an excuse to not do it Wednesday and then just do it Thursday, but Thursday already had something scheduled, so now I missed that day. I don't like doing that. The most consistency I have in my life is with working out and work, and as long as I can stay on the same routine every single day, then I just don't miss days. There's no decisions to be made, so I think one big thing that is missing in sales, whether you're doing this by yourself or you have a team, because I hear it all the time, is that oh, we only train once a week. We only train every other week. We train 2 days a week. Just do the same thing every day. And if you want to get better at sales, at acquisitions, at wholesaling, at dispo, at underwriting, like you just have to do it every single day. It doesn't have to be for hours on end. Even if you could do 20-30 minutes before you get started with your day, that's going to help you get better with whatever you are doing. So, our morning meeting schedule. So, I get to the office around 7:30, and my team gets here a little bit before 8:00. From 9:00 is when we do our training. In my office, I train acquisitions and I train dispo at the same time, and those trainings go about an hour long. We hit the phones from 9:00 until whenever they want to take their lunch. We kind of scatter lunches around noon or 1:00, and then they're back on the phones until 5:00 or 6:00, depending on if they're on a call or not. So, they are on the phones for basically 8 hours a day is their work day. Um they're here for 9 hours minimum, but an hour of that is training. So, Monday morning is our KPI day. So, for KPIs, we want to go over the previous week, what we hit, what we did not hit, and why. So, my team has a KPI sheet that they fill out every single day. Did they hit their KPIs for the day? If they didn't, what are the reasons why, and what do they need help with? So, the purpose of these meetings is really to keep you or your team focused and sharp. Every meeting has a purpose, so everybody comes prepared with notebooks and a pen in hand to take notes. Everybody is prepared, and if you show up unprepared, you're just wasting everybody's time, so we don't allow that, and nobody does it anyway, so it's not that big of a deal. KPI reviewing goals. So, let me go over the KPIs in general first. So, on acquisitions, our KPIs is to make a minimum of 65 dials per day, achieve at least 3 hours 45 minutes of talk time per day, and submit three offers per day in that sales job on acquisitions. Execute three signed contracts per week, okay? So, if those are the KPIs, there is an average throughout the week that we go over on Monday. So, they fill out their KPI sheet all week, and then Monday through Friday, and then that next Monday, we all go over our KPIs. We average them out for those 5 days in the week, and we see if everybody hit their minimums. And these are just minimum KPIs that they need to hit daily in this role. And you should be hitting these as well. With the right lead flow, you should be hitting this in an 8-hour day if you're taking this serious. Now, they are required to hit three of four of these on average throughout the week. So, if they had a bad week of dials, they can make up for it in talk time, offers, and signed contracts. If the outcome we're looking for is signed contracts anyway, that's why that is a KPI. If they can get three signed contracts, but maybe they didn't have the average talk time that they were supposed to get, but maybe their dials were way up. videos.transcript: All right. What I want to go over today is common RDRs. What are RDRs? They're reactionary defense responses. Now, these are not necessarily objections because it's something somebody says typically in the first couple minutes of a conversation. This happens usually in the intro of our process and our script. Now, an RDR, you can look at it as I always refer to the bike shop I owned for 15 years. When somebody would walk in, I would always say, "Hey, how you doing? How can I help you today?" and they would always say, "Hey, I'm just looking around." It's just a reactionary defense response. Even if they're there specifically to buy five bikes for their family, they're always going to say, "Hey, I'm just looking around." They kind of put their guard up. They don't want to feel intimidated. They don't want to feel like a used car salesman's coming after them. And they maybe just need time to kind of marinate and think and and actually look around. But it's not really a objection yet, right? they're just saying something probably because they're getting a million of these phone calls and they just don't want their time wasted. So, we don't spend a ton of time trying to overcome an RDR. We just have something in our script which we mostly refer to to overcome the RDR. So, I'm going to go over a few five of them actually of common RDRs we hear on our leads when we're first trying to get through an intro. Something somebody will say as a reactionary defense response. Again, we're not going to spend a ton of time overcoming these. We're just going to touch on them and then we're going to move on. We're going to acknowledge, address, and overcome them. Okay? I have some of these responses written down and I also have the script in my hand so I can refer back to the script so you guys know exactly what we say with these common RDRs from a seller. The first one I see, hurry up, just give me an offer. This is probably the most common one.
